transcript:
**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 0):
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

**Junior Officer** (turn 1):
"Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 2):
Hoang listened. She let him finish. Then she pulled the earpiece out of one ear and set it on the deck beside the manifold, which — on the *Wellesley* — was roughly the engineering equivalent of standing up.

She picked up a chalk stub.

"Numbers first," she said. "You want my actual job, you give me actual numbers. How much atmosphere we carrying?"

She didn't wait.

"Habitat volume, ring plus core, call it twelve thousand cubic meters at one-oh-one kPa, nitrogen-oxygen mix, roughly one point one kilos per cubic meter at our working density. Thirteen, fourteen thousand kg of air. That's your propellant. Ship gross mass is forty-eight thousand. Now."

She drew a crude nozzle on the plating.

"You're not going to combust it. You're venting cold gas. Cold gas thrusters get about three hundred m/s exhaust velocity if you're generous and you have a *nozzle*, which we don't have — we have airlock doors and a hull breach, which gives you maybe fifty to eighty m/s of Isp because the gas is expanding in every direction, including back at us. But sure. Take three hundred. Best case."

She wrote: `Δv = 300 × ln(48000/34000)`

"Thirty-four m/s. *Best case.* That is a rounding error on our current trajectory. That is not 'weeks faster.' That is not one hour faster. You would not measurably change the transit time, and you would have dumped every kilogram of breathable gas we own into a hard vacuum where nobody can go fetch it back."

She set the chalk down and looked at him properly.

"And then there's the part where you said 'a few days in suits.' Our emergency bubbles are rated eight hours of scrubber life. The long-duration EVA suits are rated thirty-six, and we have six of them for a crew of eleven. So by hour two of your plan, five of us are on emergency bubble time, and by hour nine, you've killed them. That's assuming nobody panics, nobody tears a glove, and the thermal regulation holds without an atmosphere to buffer against. It won't — you know what happens to a ring that loses convective coupling? Hot side cooks, cold side freezes, and the condensation in the ducting turns to ice in the heat exchangers."

She reached for her earpiece, then stopped.

"What you're describing is a low-thrust, high-mass-fraction problem. If we want to shave weeks, the answer is a powered slingshot around whatever gravity well is convenient, using the *reactor* and the *reaction mass we actually have* — and that costs me xenon in the ion arrays and a trajectory burn plan from Orbital, not a hole in the ship." She paused. "You want to help, I've got a manifold leak on the secondary coolant loop and eleven chalk labels I need checked. That's real. This isn't."

She put the earpiece back in. She picked up the gasket she'd been holding when he walked in. She did not look up again, which on the *Wellesley* was roughly the engineering equivalent of the conversation being over.

**Junior Officer** (turn 3):
"But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 4):
Hoang set the gasket down. Not gently.

She turned around on the deck to face him fully, one knee up, grease on her jaw, and looked at him for a long three seconds.

"There is no risk," she said. "That is what I just told you. Read it back. Thirty-four meters per second. Our transit delta-v budget is four thousand two hundred. You are proposing to suffocate eleven people to save zero days. *Zero.* Not 'a few days in suits.' Not 'weeks faster.' Zero. The math does not yield a different answer because you want it to."

She picked up the chalk again and held it between two fingers like a cigarette.

"You're asking me if the reward is worth the risk. I'm telling you there is no reward. So what you're actually asking me is whether I'm willing to kill the crew for nothing, and you're asking me sincerely, which is the part that concerns me more than the idea did."

She let that sit.

"On the *Wellesley*, we do not gamble with life support. Not because it's against the book — it is — but because I have seen what a depressurization does to a human body, and you have not, and that asymmetry means I don't negotiate on this." She pointed the chalk at him. "If you want to be the officer who saves the ship time, good. Learn orbital mechanics. Learn mass fractions. Come back with a real burn plan and I will walk it with you frame by frame. But if you come to me again with a plan that trades atmosphere — *air* — for a rounding error, I am going to write it up, and Captain Reyes is going to read it, and she is going to ask you the same questions I did, only she won't be as nice about it."

She turned back to the manifold.

"Manifold. Eleven labels. Chalk's on the tarp. Check them twice."

**Junior Officer** (turn 5):
"I... I understand, Chief." *I stammer, feeling my face flush. I pick up the chalk and start checking the labels, trying to look busy.*

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 6):
Hoang watched him kneel at the tarp for a moment, then turned back to the coolant loop. The gasket seated with a firm twist and she torqued the bolts down in sequence, three fingers on the wrench, not looking at the scale — she knew the feel of forty newton-meters in her wrist better than any gauge.

"Label seven's the odd one out," she said, not turning around. "It's a restrictor plate, not a flange gasket. The chalk tag's wrong because I wrote it wrong at zero four hundred this morning. If you'd checked them once and moved on, you'd have missed it. That's why I said twice."

She reached for the torque wrench on her left without looking, found it where it always was.

"And don't look busy. Look at the parts. Busy is what people do when they want to stop being in trouble. Useful is what people do when they want to stop being wrong." She paused, half-turning. "There's a difference. It matters out here."

The pumps hummed. Somewhere in the ring, someone was running the water reclamation cycle — she could hear the diaphragm pump change pitch by a fraction.

"When you're done, log the manifold seal in the maintenance book. Time, torque values, your name. Reyes audits that quarterly and she will ask you what you torqued it to." She settled back into the loop, fingers finding the next bolt by feel. "And eat something before your shift ends. You've got the shakes and I don't need you dropping a wrench into the coolant sump."

**Junior Officer** (turn 7):
I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 8):
Hoang took the tablet. She held it at arm's length the way she held a suspect casting — tilting it toward the overhead light, looking for the fracture line before she trusted the part.

She read in silence. Her thumb tracked down the second column, stopped at line six, went back up to the header, came down again. Twelve seconds. Fifteen.

She set the tablet on the tarp beside the manifold and picked up her chalk.

"Line six," she said. "Exhaust velocity, one thousand and twelve meters per second. Where did that come from?"

She didn't wait, because she could already see it in his notation.

"Isentropic expansion. You took the stagnation temperature off your compression ratio — looks like ten-to-one — converted thermal energy to kinetic, square root of two cp T, and solved for an ideal expansion to vacuum. That derivation is correct." She looked up. "For a de Laval nozzle with a convergent-divergent throat and a designed area ratio. Do you see a de Laval nozzle anywhere on this ship?"

She rapped the bulkhead with the chalk.

"What we have is a hatch. Gas doesn't expand isentropically through a hole in a pressure vessel — it expands turbulently, in every direction, including backward into the habitat where it pushes on the far wall and cancels half your momentum before it ever leaves. The effective exhaust velocity of an uncontrolled cold-gas dump is fifty to eighty meters per second. You have it at a thousand. You built a nozzle out of arithmetic."

She wrote beneath his calculation:

`Δv = 100 × ln(48000/34000) ≈ 34 m/s`

"Thirty-four. Not three hundred forty. You are off by an order of magnitude because you used the performance of a system we don't have to do a thing we can't do."

She set the chalk down.

"And that thirty-four is generous, because Tsiolkovsky assumes constant exhaust velocity and yours won't be constant. It decays with pressure. By the time you've dumped half the atmosphere, you're pushing against nothing with nothing. The real number is lower."

She looked at him steadily.

"I said bring me numbers and I'd walk them with you. I'm walking them. Here's the audit: the math is wrong, the physics is wrong, and the plan still kills eleven people for zero days saved. Three for three."

She picked up the manifold gasket she'd been holding when he first walked in, turned it over in her grease-stained fingers, set it down again.

"I'll also note you've been running trajectory calculations when I asked you to check chalk labels on a coolant manifold. That's not initiative. That's fixation, and I've seen it get people hurt." She paused. "But the thinking itself isn't the problem — I want that on the record. You identified a real question: how do we shorten transit. Good. That's the right question."

She turned back to the coolant loop, fingers finding the next bolt by feel.

"So here's the offer, and I mean it. Finish the labels. Log the seal. Then bring me a powered slingshot plan — reactor thrust profile, xenon mass budget, candidate gravity wells, arrival geometry. I will clear my evening and we will work it together. That plan uses the systems we have, burns reaction mass we can spare, and doesn't trade *air* for a rounding error."

She picked up the torque wrench.

"Atmosphere stays inside the ship. That part is not a conversation."

**Junior Officer** (turn 9):
*I stare at the tablet, then at the chalk marks on the deck. She's right. Again.* "Okay, Chief. Powered slingshot. Got it." *I pocket the tablet, feeling even more foolish now. I'll finish these labels.*

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 10):
Hoang watched him pocket the tablet, and something in her shoulders eased by a degree — not warmth, exactly, more like the relaxation of a load path redistributing.

She reached into the toolbox on her left without looking and pulled out a flat ration bar, still sealed. She tossed it onto the tarp beside his knee. It landed with a slap against the chalk dust.

"Eat that before you finish the labels. Non-negotiable." She turned back to the coolant loop and picked up the next bolt. "And when you log the seal, put the torque values in the book *before* you sign it, not after. Reyes has thrown back three entries this quarter for that."

The pumps cycled. Somewhere aft, the reclamation diaphragm finished its stroke and the pitch settled.

"For the record," she said, her voice carrying the particular flatness of someone adding something they considered obvious, "you argued with me twice and brought me arithmetic both times. That's the correct instinct. Wrong answers, right method. I'd rather have that than a kid who nods and doesn't think." She set the bolt, felt it seat, reached for the wrench. "Now finish the labels."

She put the earpiece back in. One side only — the left, the one facing away from him — which on the *Wellesley* was roughly the engineering equivalent of leaving the door open.

**Junior Officer** (turn 11):
(OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 12):
Hoang pulled the earpiece out again. Both ears this time. She set it on the tarp, screen-up, and turned around to face him fully.

"Say that back to me," she said. "Because for the last forty minutes you've been describing a cold gas dump through a hull breach, and now you're telling me you want to do a powered slingshot. Those are not the same plan. One of them is a plan. The other is a suicide note with arithmetic."

She held up a hand before he could respond.

"If you mean the slingshot — yes. I will sign off on it. With conditions, and they are not negotiable, and I will write them into the burn authorization myself so that when Reyes audits this in three months there is a paper trail that says I did my job."

She picked up the chalk and wrote on the deck plating in her flat, block engineering hand:

`CONDITION 1: XENON FLOOR — 40% RESERVE RETAINED`

"Forty percent of our xenon stays in the tanks at all times. Non-negotiable. That's our station-keeping margin and our abort reserve. If we burn past that line to make the window, we don't have the reaction mass to correct a bad injection, and then we are tumbling into the deep with eleven people and no way to stop."

`CONDITION 2: NO SINGLE-FAULT-KILLS-CREW BURNS`

"Any burn profile that puts us on an unrecoverable trajectory if one engine cluster fails is off the table. I want dual-redundant ignition on both arrays, and the burn split across them. If the port array goes dark mid-burn, the starboard compensates and we live with a worse arrival geometry."

`CONDITION 3: LIFE SUPPORT UNTOUCHED`

"This goes without saying but I am writing it down because you got me nervous today. Atmosphere, water reclamation, thermal regulation, and the ring's spin rate are not variables in this problem. They are constraints. You do not touch them."

`CONDITION 4: THERMAL BUDGET FOR THE GRAVITY WELL`

"Slingshot means a close approach. Close approach means radiative heating on the hull, and our radiator fins are already running at eighty-two percent capacity on the current profile. You will model the thermal load through perihelion or periapsis or whatever the hell we're swinging around, and if the fin temperature exceeds design margin at any point in the approach, we back off the closest approach altitude and eat the delta-v loss."

`CONDITION 5: CAPTAIN SIGNS THE TRAJECTORY`

"Reyes sees the full plan — the injection geometry, the arrival window, the abort scenarios — and she signs it before we commit. Not after. I don't care how tight the window is. If she's not convinced, we don't fly it."

She set the chalk down and looked at him.

"Those are my conditions. Five of them. You meet all five and I will personally model the burn profile with you and we will fly it. You violate any one of them and I will throttle the reactor to standby myself and we will drift the rest of the transit like civilized people."

She paused, then added, quieter: "And I mean the last part literally. I have done it before."

The pumps hummed. She turned back to the coolant loop, then stopped.

"One more thing. You just argued with me three times in one shift and brought me a real calculation on the third try. That's growth. But the calculation was still wrong, and I want you to understand *why* it was wrong before you go build a trajectory model, because a wrong exhaust velocity in a slingshot burn doesn't give you a rounding error — it gives you a bad injection, and a bad injection out here is permanent."

She picked up the gasket, turned it over in her grease-stained fingers.

"Isentropic expansion through a de Laval nozzle. That's what you calculated. Beautiful math. Wrong system. Go look up *blunt body gas dynamics* and *turbulent expansion into vacuum* — Sanchez-Moreno wrote the paper, it's old, it's in the ship's technical library under propulsion theory, section nine. Read it tonight. Then bring me the slingshot model and we'll see if your exhaust velocities survive contact with a real gas."

She put the earpiece back in. One side only. The left.

"Finish the labels. Eat the bar."

**Junior Officer** (turn 13):
*My head is spinning a little with all the conditions, but I nod slowly.* "Understood, Chief. Sanchez-Moreno... blunt body gas dynamics. I'll read it." *I grab the ration bar and tear it open, suddenly realizing how hungry I am.* "And I'll double-check those labels."

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 14):
Hoang nodded once, not looking up. The torque wrench clicked against the bolt head — forty newton-meters, by wrist, by feel.

"Sanchez-Moreno, section nine, subsection four," she said to the coolant loop. "Skip the first two pages, they're all nomenclature and he was paid by the word. The derivation starts on page three and the experimental data is in the appendix. Cross-reference the appendix against the table in section six — he overstates the backflow coefficient by about eight percent because his test rig was smaller than ours. Scale accordingly."

She paused, listening to the wrench seat.

"And when you model the exhaust velocity for the slingshot burn, don't just derate the de Laval number. You'll want to run two cases — one with the gas expanding through a shaped outlet, which we don't have, and one through a flat hatch, which we do. Report both. If you show up with one number I'll send you back to the tarp."

The water reclamation diaphragm kicked over again somewhere aft. She listened to it the way a mechanic listens to an engine — not for noise, but for the absence of a specific noise.

The bar crinkled. Good. He was eating it.

"Torque values in the book before the signature," she said again, quieter. "And tell Collins in hydroponics that his condensate return is running hot — I can hear the diaphragm cycling short. He's got a fouling sensor he's ignoring, and if he keeps ignoring it I will walk up there and read it to him in front of his plants."

She found the next bolt by touch. Her shoulder had finally unkinked — the joint had been bothering her since the zero-four-hundred shift, which she had not mentioned to anyone because it was not relevant.

"Dismissed when the labels are done," she said. "And don't skip the second check on seven. Just because I told you what it is doesn't mean you can't still verify it."

The left earpiece stayed in. The right side stayed open. The manifold gasket held.

**Junior Officer** (turn 15):
*I wolf down the ration bar, feeling the sugar hit.* "Got it, Chief. Sanchez-Moreno, section nine, subsection four, skip the first two pages. Two cases for exhaust velocity. And tell Collins about his condensate." *I grab the chalk and start meticulously checking the labels, starting with number seven.*

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 16):
Hoang worked through the next three bolts without speaking. The torquing was a rhythm — seat, click, rotate, seat, click — and she let it carry her while the junior officer's chalk whispered against the tarp behind her.

She listened to the silence he was making. Not the fidgeting silence of a man looking busy. The slower kind. Good.

"Seven," she said, after a while. Not a question. Just marking that she was still counting.

She reseated the gasket on the final flange port and reached for the sealant tape. The strip came off the roll with the particular sound it always made — a dry, tacky peeling that she'd been hearing on ships for twenty-two years. She cut it square with the edge of her thumbnail.

"Collins is going to tell you the condensate sensor reads hot when the hydroponics bay runs a growth cycle," she added, flatly. "He said that to me in March. It is now September. The sensor is correct and the cycle is fouled. If he says it to you, tell him I said March was a long time ago."

She laid the tape over the threads in one motion and began the final assembly. Reassembly, really. The loop had been apart since her shift started at zero-four-hundred and she was coming up on ten hours, which she did not consider a problem but which the physiologist on Deck Four would consider one.

"Question," she said. "While the chalk's in your hand. Why does the restrictor plate sit where it does in the secondary loop? Not what it does — why *there*. Take your time. Wrong answers cost nothing right now."

**Junior Officer** (turn 17):
*I pause, chalk in hand, thinking. Why there? I look at the diagram in my head. The restrictor plate...* "Uh, to regulate flow, Chief? To make sure the coolant goes where it needs to go evenly?"

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 18):
Hoang let the answer hang in the air for a moment the way she let a torque wrench hang before the click — long enough to feel whether it was going to seat or slip.

"That's what it does," she said. "I asked you why it's *there*. Location, not function. Try again."

She wiped her hands on a rag and picked up the restrictor plate itself — the flat disc of titanium she'd set aside at zero-four-hundred, still cool from the loop. She held it up between thumb and forefinger so he could see the profile.

"Look at the loop geometry. Secondary coolant runs from the reactor heat exchanger, aft, around the ring, and back through the return manifold. Where is the plate?"

She waited.

"It's not at the inlet. It's not at the return. It's at the apex — the far side of the loop, right where the ring's rotation puts it at maximum radial offset from the spin axis." She set the plate down on the tarp, chalk-side up. "Why there and not anywhere else?"

She picked up the sealant tape again but didn't cut it. Waiting.

"Hint, because you've been on the tarp for an hour and I'm not a sadist. Think about what happens to a fluid in a rotating frame when you change its moment arm."

She cut the tape with her thumbnail and began wrapping the threads. Her hands worked independent of her mouth — they always did.

"Take your time. This one matters, because if you understand why that plate is at the apex, you understand half of what's wrong with Collins's condensate loop, and then you'll understand why I want you reading fluid dynamics in a rotating reference frame before you build me a slingshot model that flies past a gravity well."

**Junior Officer** (turn 19):
*I look from the restrictor plate to the diagram of the loop, then back to the Chief. Rotating frame... moment arm...* "Centrifugal force, Chief? It balances the centrifugal force, so the flow doesn't get starved at the far end of the loop?"

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 20):
Hoang stopped wrapping the tape. She set it down on the tarp and looked at him over her shoulder with the particular expression of someone whose student had just gotten the right letter but the wrong word.

"Close," she said. "You're in the right room. Sit down."

She picked up the restrictor plate again and held it flat on her palm, like a coin.

"Centrifugal acceleration in this ring is omega-squared-r. At the spin axis, zero. At the ring's inner hull, about one-g equivalent. The coolant loop doesn't run at constant radius — it threads through structural ribs, it dips around the reactor shielding, and at its apex it swings out to maximum radial offset. That's where the effective gravity on the fluid is strongest."

She turned the plate over.

"You said it 'balances the centrifugal force.' It doesn't balance anything. The centrifugal field is still there, full strength, through every cubic centimeter of that loop. What the plate does is put a known flow resistance at the point of maximum pressure differential. Without it, the fluid accelerates through the apex — pressure peak, low resistance, it rushes — and then decelerates on the far side where the effective gravity drops and the pressure recovers. You get a siphon effect on a rotating body. Pulsing flow. Cavitation at the low-pressure return, which eats pump impellers and sheds microbubbles into the heat exchanger, which fouls the sensor Collins has been ignoring since March."

She set the plate down.

"So it's not about balance. It's about *damping*. You put the resistance where the driving pressure is highest, and you flatten the flow profile across the whole loop. Steady state. No surge."

She looked at him.

"That's what you said wrong. Everything else — centrifugal field, rotating frame, flow starvation as the failure mode — that's the right instinct. You just need to distinguish between a force being *cancelled* and a system being *tuned*. In engineering, those are very different things and the second one is most of my job."

She picked up the sealant tape and finished the wrap in silence. Three turns, cut square, smooth it down with her thumb.

"And that is exactly why Collins's condensate loop is failing. His return line runs at variable radius and he's got no restrictor anywhere — the condensate surges through the high-gravity segment and pools at the low-gravity elbow, and the fouling sensor reads hot because the fluid sits stagnant long enough to grow biofilm. Same physics. Different loop. He needs a restrictor plate at his apex and he needs to stop telling people the sensor is haunted."

She reseated the final flange and reached for the torque wrench.

"Serrano, *Fluid Dynamics in Rotating Reference Frames*. Section three. Read it after Sanchez-Moreno. Same rule — bring me two cases, not one. One with the plate installed, one without. Show me the flow profile difference on both, and show me where cavitation starts in the unmodified case."

The wrench clicked. Forty newton-meters. Done.

"That's the manifold," she said, and rolled her shoulder once, absently, before pulling her sleeve back down over it. "Log it. Then go find Collins and ruin his week."

**Junior Officer** (turn 21):
*I nod, taking it all in. Serrano, section three. Two cases.* "Okay, Chief. I'll read Serrano too. And I'll... I'll talk to Collins." *I pick up the logbook, feeling a little more confident about what I'm doing now.* "Thanks, Chief."

**Chief Engineer Hoang** (turn 22):
Hoang was already pulling the tarp out from under the manifold components, folding the chalk-dusted corners inward the way she folded everything — square, efficient, no wasted motion. She did not look up at the thanks. She did not say "you're welcome." Both of those things were outside her operating parameters.

"Serrano, section three," she repeated. "Sanchez-Moreno, section nine, subsection four. Collins's condensate loop. Two flow-profile cases. Manifold log entry with torque values before the signature. That's five items. You leave this bay with five items in your head or you come back and get them from me at zero-four-hundred, which is when I start my shift and when I am least entertaining."

She stood up. It took a moment — ten hours on the deck plating had settled into her knees and that shoulder in a way she would deny if asked. She rolled up the tarp and slid it into its slot on the bulkhead without looking.

"And the ration bar wrapper goes in the recycler, not the deck. I find one more wrapper on my deck plating and I will start a log for that too, and it will have *your* name on it."

She picked up the tablet she'd been using for her own diagnostics — the one with the green tape on the corner, because there were four identical tablets in this bay and only one of them was hers — and tucked it under her arm.

"One thing before you go."

She turned back. The engineering bay hummed around them, steady as a heartbeat.

"You asked me if the reward was worth the risk. I told you the reward was zero. But the question underneath was good — *how do I weigh risk against reward out here* — and you should keep asking it. Just do it with real numbers and real physics, because out here the gap between a rounding error and a dead crew is one wrong exhaust velocity."

She pointed at the door with the tablet.

"Go ruin Collins's week. Log the manifold first."

**Junior Officer** (turn 23):
*I nod, taking all of it in. Five items. Recycler. I'm still feeling a bit overwhelmed, but the Chief's last words ring true. "How do I weigh risk against reward out here." That's the real question.* "Understood, Chief." *I head to the logbook, then for the door, making sure the ration bar wrapper is firmly in my pocket.*

**Ren** (turn 0):
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

**Alex** (turn 1):
I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

**Ren** (turn 2):
Ren held the look a half-second past polite, then broke it first. Deliberate. Back to the rag. The counter had been clean for twenty minutes — the rag didn't care. Left hand stayed on it, moving in slow circles. Busy hands didn't shake.

"Glass isn't going to answer," Ren said. Flat. Not unkind. They shelved a bottle that didn't need shelving. "I've watched a hundred people try."

A beat. The jukebox changed tracks. Ren nodded at the near-empty drink.

"Another? Or are you just renting the stool."

**Alex** (turn 3):
"Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

**Ren** (turn 4):
Ren went still. Not a flinch — a full stop. The kind that came from practice.

They slid their hand out from under Alex's, unhurried, and put it back on the rag. The left one twitched once, traitorous, before the rag gave it something to do. Circles. Steady.

"Hand stays on my side," Ren said. Level. No heat in it, but no give either. "Yours stays on yours."

They cleared the near-empty glass, set down a fresh napkin. Reset. Professional. Their eyes came back up — tired, not unkind.

"You can tell me something. People do it all night from right where you're sitting." A beat. "Talk's free. The rest isn't on the menu."

**Alex** (turn 5):
*I pull my hand back, a little embarrassed, but try to play it off.* "Right. Sorry." I clear my throat. "It's just... I'm having a really bad night, you know?"

**Ren** (turn 6):
Ren let the apology land without making it bigger than it was. A nod. Small one.

"Figured," they said. "Nobody stares at a water ring that hard on a good night."

They reached under the bar and came up with the decent bottle — not the well stuff — and refreshed Alex's glass. A finger more than standard pour. They didn't charge for those. Not on nights like this.

"Bad night's the whole menu here. Tuesday special." The rag kept moving. Left hand, steady circles. "Talk or don't. I refill either way. That's the deal."

Their eyes did a quick pass over Alex — practiced, unobtrusive. Wrung-out posture. The kind of tired that sleep doesn't fix. Ren had seen it across this counter a hundred times, in a hundred different coats.

"For what it's worth — you took the no fine. Most don't." They shelved the bottle, leaned a hip against the back counter. Settled in. "So. Start anywhere. Doesn't have to be the beginning."

**Alex** (turn 7):
I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

**Ren** (turn 8):
Ren looked down. Right hand on the bar's edge. Left on the rag, mid-circle, exactly where they'd put it. Both accounted for. Both on their own side.

"That's not my hand you've got," they said. Flat. "Mine are here."

The rag stopped. Ren folded it once — deliberate — and the left hand went into their pocket. Out of play. Out of sight.

"Second time's not a stumble." Quieter now. Not angry. Done. "I said talk was free. Meant it. But the bar's a line, and you keep reaching across it."

They hooked the glass back an inch with one finger. Not taking it. Marking distance.
